question.leadin: Give the following about the decolonization of Africa.
question.text: This former French colony's National Liberation Front, or FLN, won its independence in an eight-year war that ended with the Evian Accords.
question.clue: A nuclear test named "blue jerboa" was carried out near this colony's town of Reggane.

swap.leadin: Name these dictators who are still alive.
swap.text: This Libyan outlined his philosophies in the Green Book. He also released the Lockerbie bomber and, in a United Nations speech, suggested partitioning Switzerland.
swap.clue: After protests against this man's rule began, a rebel government was established in the city of Benghazi (ben-GAH-zee).

question.leadin: Name these countries in sub-Sarahan Africa with large populations belonging to the Bantu ethnic groups in Sub-Saharan Africa.
question.text: This country is approximately three-fourths Bantu, with almost twenty three percent being Zulu. Before becoming this country's first black president, Nelson Mandela was a Xhosa (KOH-sa) -speaking lawyer in Johannesburg.
question.clue: In that song, musicians pledged to not play at a casino resort in this country, "Sun City".

swap.leadin: Give the following about African Nobel Peace Prize laureates.
swap.text: This South African anti-apartheid leader was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993, three years after he was freed from Robben Island prison and a year before he became South Africa's first freely elected president.
swap.clue: The first of this person's attempts to earn a bachelor's degree ended after a protest regarding a canteen worker, while their future LLB studies were influenced by their friendship withWalter Sisulu ("see-SOO-loo").

question.leadin: The Simba Rebellion was part of a 1960s crisis in this modern-day country.
question.text: Identify this former Belgian colony whose first post-independence prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, was executed in its breakaway region of Katanga.
question.answerHtml: Democratic Republic of the Congo [or DRC; or Congo-Kinshasa; do not accept “Republic of the Congo”; prompt on “Congo”]
question.clue: A Luba chieftain led a split of one party in this country into the MNC-L and the MNC-K before leading the brief secessionist state South-Kasai, while Moise Tshombe led this country's secessionist Katanga province.

swap.leadin: Dag Hammarskjold died in a plane crash en route to negotiations with this region's leader.
swap.text: Name this region of the Congo that became a breakaway state under Moise Tshombe in 1960.
swap.clue: It issued its own stamps and had a 16-plane airforce commanded by Jan Zumbach.

question.text: This African nation also resisted European colonization under charismatic muslim leaders like the Mahdi, but was decisively crushed at the Battle of Omdurman. Mahdist forces had also helped retake Khartoum, leading to the death of Chinese Gordon.
question.clue: A year after that clash, Abdullah al-Taashi was killed here at Umm Diwaykarat.

swap.leadin: Name these African leaders of freedom movements.
swap.text: This white Prime Minister of Rhodesia unilaterally declared independence from Britain, after which Robert Mugabe was elected president of Zimbabwe.
swap.clue: His tenure ended with the Internal Settlement, under which he was replaced by Bishop Abel Muzorewa, and soon after, he was definitively removed by the Lancaster House Conference.

question.leadin: This country was led by the Marxist-leaning president Samora Machel until his 1986 death in a mysterious plane crash.
question.text: Name this African country where the FRELIMO and RENAMO parties fought a protracted civil war.
question.clue: A right-wing organization opposing the socialist government of this country drew support from such cities as the Beira port in Sofala province, was formed by Andre Matsangaissa, and laid down its arms in the 1990s following the Rome Accords.

swap.text: The Almoravids were based in Marrakesh, a city in this modern-day country. This country was also the home of the Almohads and various other Berber tribes.
swap.clue: In the 11th century a Berber chieftain built its city of Marrakesh.

question.text: This Namibian ethnic group was targeted in an 1904-1908 genocide led by Lothar von Trotha along with the related Namaqua people. Women of this ethnic group often wear traditional German blouses and dresses.
question.clue: This ethnic group that was subject to a genocide by Lothar von Trotha. This people was unable to wage war after they lost their main force at the Battle of Waterberg.

swap.text: The raid at Entebbe occurred in this African country led by Idi Amin. This country is the site of a civil war fought against the Lord's Resistance Army.
swap.clue: The issuance of the Common Man's Charter in this country was part of a socialist doctrine called the Move to the Left, which also involved taking control of sixty percent of eighty corporations after the Nakivubo Pronouncement.

question.leadin: In the early 18th century, this empire recruited scouts to clear brush, blaze false trails, and drain standing water based on medical expertise that included a precursor of germ theory.
question.text: Name this empire whose founder Osei Tutu ("OH-say TOO-too") modernized its army with tactics he learned from the Akwamuhene ("ah-KWAH-moo-hay-nay"). Many houses had indoor plumbing in this empire's city of Kumasi.
question.clue: This state's unifier founded his capital on the site where a Kum tree planted by the priest Okomfo Anokyo prospered; that king, who also defeated the Denkyira, was Osei Tutu.

swap.leadin: According to al-Umari, the central participant of this event did not want to meet with the Mamluk sultan al-Malik al-Nasir because he would be obligated to kiss the ground and the sultan's hand.
swap.text: Name this event, during which a ruler of the Mali Empire devastated the economy of Cairo for twelve years through his generosity by giving out and spending a massive amount of gold.
swap.answerHtml: Mansa Musa’s hajj [or Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage to Mecca, or anything indicating Mansa Musa going to Mecca; prompt on partial answers]
swap.clue: Some architects who returned from this event helped build new structures in Gao.

question.text: The rinderpest epizootic weakened the forces of Hendrik Witbooi ("VUT-boy"), setting the stage for this first genocide of the 20th century. Germans under Lothar von Trotha carried out this genocide of two ethnic groups in modern-day Namibia.
question.answerHtml: Herero and Namaqua genocide [or Völkermord an den Herero und Nama; accept Ovaherero for “Herero”; prompt on Herero genocide or Namaqua genocide; prompt on Khoekhoe for “Nama”] (Among other disastrous impacts, the 1890s rinderpest epizootic is also linked to the deaths of two-thirds of the Maasai and the spread of the tsetse fly.)

swap.text: In contrast to Houphouet-Boigny's close relationship with France, this first leader of Guinea led his country in rejecting a 1958 referendum for self governance within the French empire. In April 2019, this man's son Mohamed was convicted in Texas for enslaving a Guinean girl for 16 years.
swap.clue: This author of the collection "Militant Poems" gained infamy for using Camp Boiro National Guard Barracks as a political prison, executing over 50,000 people, sparking a naval attack on his capital by Portuguese troops in 1970.

question.leadin: The Glorious Victories chronicles Amda Seyon's conquest of Islamic Ifat from this sultanate's founding Walashma dynasty, which aided Hadiya after Zara Yaqob forcibly converted Princess Eleni.
question.text: Name this sultanate that fortified its "holy city" of Harar after Lebna Dengel allied Ethiopia with Portugal to fight its Afar and Somali forces. It was based north of the Ajuran Empire.
question.answerHtml: Adal Sultanate [or Adäl Kingdom or Adäl Empire or Bar Sa‘d ad-Dīn; accept Adel or Adalite in place of “Adal”; accept Ethiopian–Adäl War or Abyssinian–Adäl War] (Nur ibn Mujahid fortified Harar.)
question.clue: This sultanate located on the western shores of the Gulf of Aden. Its general Ahmad Ibrahim al-Ghazi led several successful campaigns against Ethiopia and killed Emperor Dawit II.

swap.text: The German explorer Heinrich Barth preserved two copies of the Girgam, the over eight centuries long king list of this empire whose capitals included Ngazargamu [in-GAHZ-ar-GAH-moo] and Kukawa [koo-KAH-wah].
swap.clue: One important mai or king of this nation named Hummay converted it to Islam and founded the Sayfawa dynasty.

question.text: This institution first perpetuated the Tutsi-dominant beliefs of Leon-Paul Classe, then supported the Bahutu Manifesto's call for an end to Hutu discrimination. This institution abetted the massacre, then bulldozing, of 20,000 civilians in Nyarubuye during the Genocide.
question.answerHtml: Roman Catholic Church in Rwanda [prompt on Christian Church]

swap.leadin: This city's kings list, the Song of Bagauda, describes the war that its sarki Muhammad Rumfa waged with Katsina.
swap.text: Name this most powerful of the seven Hausa city-states of modern-day Nigeria, whose Kurmi market was an endpoint of Trans-Saharan trade.
swap.clue: This city in northern Nigeria has been the major center of Hausa culture since the 10th century, as related by its namesake Chronicle of Hausa history. This city became the capital of a Fulani emirate after 1805.
